          Reading your nervous system

          Your nervous system is always running your life and typically you're completely unaware of it.

          You wake up feeling drained or maybe panicky. You're snapping at people for no reason. You're working hard and accomplishing nothing. You're tired but can't sleep. You're numb and you don't know why.

          These aren't personality traits. They aren't moods. They're conscious experiences of nervous system states. The difference between being at the mercy of them and being able to work with them is whether you can read them. To understand them.

          This is the page where you learn to read.

          Not how you should read. Not what your states ought to be. Just how to recognize, in your own body, in real time, what's actually happening. You connect with what's actually happening so you can stop fighting yourself and start working with what's actually there.

          This page is the second in a three-page series. The first, The Polyvagal Current, introduces the model: three circles representing your primary autonomic states (ventral, sympathetic, dorsal) flowing in a continuous current, plus a Safety Influence slider that determines whether each state shows up regulated (Safety, Play, Stillness) or dysregulated (Shutdown, Freeze, Fight-or-Flight). If you haven't read that one, start there. This page assumes you have.

          What you'll get here: a daily nervous system literacy practice. The four columns of the Current in the model above (Cognitions, Emotions, Sensations, Impulses) and how to use them as observation doors into your own state. How to recognize where you are on the slider in real time. How to notice when the current is shifting. The regulated states most people have never been taught to recognize. What to do when your usual reading columns are blocked. And the longer arc: how nervous system literacy deepens over months and years.

          This isn't a hack. It's a practice. Slow at first, fluent over time. Nothing about it requires special training, expensive equipment, or anyone's permission. You're learning to pay attention to a system that's been talking to you your whole life. The only new piece is the vocabulary.

          Quick orientation

          What state is my nervous system in?

          The short answer: one of three.

          You have three primary autonomic states: ventral (engaged, connected), sympathetic (mobilized), and dorsal (immobilized). One of them is dominant right now. Which one depends on what's happening in your body and how much safety is in your system. The Safety Influence slider on the Polyvagal Current determines whether the dominant state shows up in its regulated form (Safety, Play, Stillness) or its stuck form (Shutdown, Freeze, Fight-or-Flight).

          To tell which state you're in, you read four observable signals: your thoughts, your emotions, your body's sensations, and your action impulses. Those are the four columns shown on this page's version of the Current.

          Whichever one is loudest in this moment is your door in. A quick scan of all four takes about thirty seconds and gives you a working read of the dominant state.

          The rest of this page is how to make that read fast, accurate, and habitual.

          The doorways

          The four columns as observational doorways

          The version of the Polyvagal Current shown on this page includes four columns underneath the model: Cognitions, Emotions, Sensations, Impulses. They're the literacy layer; what you actually use to read which circle is dominant and where the Safety Influence slider is sitting right now. Anything you experience that tells you what state you're in shows up in one of these four columns.

          Think of them as four doors into the same room. If you can't get in through the cognitive door, maybe the sensation door is unlocked. If you can't name the emotion, maybe you can name the impulse. The same state can be read through any of the four and different people read themselves through different primary columns.

          Typically, I teach clients and Unstucking Academy students how to use their Emotions as the doorway to their inner world. Stuck Not Broken: Book 3 also details this process.

          Cognitions
          The thoughts themselves. Not the content so much as the pattern and flavor. Are your thoughts racing or slow? Narrow or broad? Catastrophic or balanced? Fixated on one thing or able to hold several? If your thoughts just got more urgent and tunnel-visioned, that's sympathetic data, the slider sliding down. If they just got foggy and slow, that's dorsal data without much safety. If they got curious and balanced, that's ventral coming online.
          Emotions
          The conscious, named feeling experience. The things you'd report if someone asked. Anxious? Numb? Connected? Irritated? Calm? Playful? Each named emotion is the surface of a state. Anxiety, urgency, anger → sympathetic without enough safety. Sad, numb, hopelessness → dorsal without enough safety. Caring, playfulness, curiosity → safety is in the system and the branches are sorting into their regulated forms.
          Sensations
          The felt, somatic experience of emotions. Warmth or cold. Tightness or openness. Speed (heart, breath) or slowness. Weight (heavy, leaden) or lightness. Buzzing, tingling, pressure, relaxation. Sensations are a doorway most have lost access to. The sensation door can be reopened with practice.
          Impulses
          What your body wants to do. The action urges. Want to leave? Want to hide? Want to connect? Want to fix? Want to fight? Want to disappear? Impulses are typically the most difficult to access and only surface when deeply connected to the body and listening with patience and compassion. Day-to-day reflexive impulses are useful information as well, like the urge to leave a difficult conversation.

          How to use them: you don't need all four. You need one you can get in through. Start with whichever feels most accessible.

          A practical pattern: scan briefly across the four columns. Which one is loudest? Saying, "Hey, check me out"? That's your door in. Use it to read which circle of the Current is dominant right now, and roughly where the safety slider sits. Then check the other three. The more columns align, the more confident your read.

          This isn't an interrogation. Not a test. It's a curious focus of attention. Spend a few seconds. The columns aren't a worksheet. They're a habit of noticing.

          Find your door

          Start where you can. Which column is easiest?

          Most people have one column they can read clearly (usually cognitions), two they can read partially (usually emotions and impulses), and one that's mostly closed off (usually sensations). That's normal. Different histories build different access.

          A few common patterns:

          If you're highly analytical, cognitions are usually your easiest column. You can tell what your thoughts are doing before you can name your emotions. Start there. Read your thought patterns, like racing, narrow, fixated, foggy, or balanced. Then use that read to make educated guesses about the other columns until they become more obvious.

          If you're emotionally fluent, emotions are usually the easiest door. You can name what you're feeling before you can read your body's more subtle internal signals. Start there. Name the emotion, then trace it to a state, then check the other columns.

          If you grew up in a body-aware family or have done somatic work, sensations are usually your strongest door. You can feel your heart speeding up, subtle tingles of your state shifting, a clenched jaw, or expansion in your chest.

          If you know your body chronically wants to do something, start with impulses. "I always want to leave!" "I feel like collapsing all the time." Find the impulse, name the state, then check the other domains.

          A few practical tips for opening closed experiential doors over time:

          Borrow from one column to find another. If you've named an emotion, ask: where in my body do I feel this? Even a vague answer ("my chest is tight, maybe?") is progress. Doors open by being used.

          Lower the bar. You don't need to know. It's okay to make your best guess. For now, practice. Over time, you'll get more precise and it'll feel more natural.

          Track in writing, briefly. Not deep insight journaling. One or two short notes a day. "Foggy this morning, didn't want to talk, head felt heavy." Over weeks, patterns emerge that you couldn't see in real time.

          Use the visual. Pull up The Polyvagal Current, watch the three circles, look at where the safety slider sits. Compare to your own experience right now. Repetition over time strengthens the link between the model and your felt sense.

          The point isn't perfect access.

          The point is some access, getting deeper over time. Start with one column. The others come online as the literacy builds.

          The practice

          Daily check-ins: how to actually read your nervous system

          The practice itself is simple. The trick is making it sustainable, not looking for a hack or performative self-exploration.

          Morning check-in (30 seconds). Before you start a busy day, take half a minute. What state did I wake up in? Which column is the most obvious? You don't have to act on it. You're just noticing. If you wake up in dorsal, knowing that changes how you'd approach the morning. If you wake up sympathetic, knowing that changes how much you'll trust the urgent thoughts.

          Mid-day check-in (30 seconds). Sometime in the middle of the day, ideally before a transition (lunch, end of a meeting, between tasks), check again. Where am I now? Has the current shifted since this morning? Which direction is the safety slider moving? Attaching this to a mid-day ritual might be ideal.

          Evening check-in (30 seconds). End of the day. Where am I now? What state did I spend most of the day in? What shifted it? How can I tell using the Current's four columns?

          That's a realistic practice. Ninety seconds across the day. The point isn't depth, the point is frequency. Brief, repeated attention beats occasional deep dives. Even one 30 second ritual with your coffee every morning is better than nothing and can have real benefits to emotional regulation.

          A few principles to keep in mind:

          Don't fix what you find. When you check in, you might notice something uncomfortable. Don't immediately try to "regulate" it. First, just name it. Reading and regulating are two different practices. This page is the reading. Regulation comes later, and often the naming alone can subtly shift things.

          Don't grade yourself. There's no good or bad state to find. Shutdown or flight/fight aren't failures. For now, they're information. Something you can continue to build on.

          Notice changes, not just states. State changes are often more informative than absolute states. I just got narrower. I just got heavier. My breathing relaxed into my belly. Those shifts tell you what just happened and that can give you hints about you might be reacting to, whether an external cue or simply from noticing your internal world with curiosity. The Polyvagal Current is, by definition, always moving. You're reading the movement.

          Use the language out loud. "I'm in stuck fight-or-flight right now." "I'm sliding toward dorsal." Saying it to yourself or to a co-regulative someone tends to make things a bit more real versus keeping it quietly in your own mind. It helps shift things from permanent brokenness into temporary stuckness.

          Pair it with something existing. If you already drink coffee in the morning, your morning check-in goes with the coffee. If you already brush your teeth at night, your evening check-in goes with the toothbrush. Don't add a new ritual; piggyback on a current one.

          Ninety seconds, three times a day, paired with existing habits. (Or less.) That's a practice you can realistically implement. No extra time. No extra demands. Just a touch more presence and curiosity.

          The other half

          Recognizing the regulated states

          Most people have been taught what stress feels like. They've been taught what burnout feels like. They have a better vocabulary for dysregulation and an almost empty vocabulary for regulation. Nervous system literacy means closing that gap.

          In the Polyvagal Current, every autonomic state has a regulated expression. This is the version that shows up when there's enough safety in the system. Here's what each looks like in detail. Learn to recognize these in yourself, and you'll know when you're regulated. When you recognize regulation, you can make a conscious choice to mindfully experience it, thereby deepening it.

          Ventral vagal safety

          The ventral vagal safety state is the one that most people think of when they want to have more happiness and calm in their life. With enough safety in the system, it repurposes the defensive states into something else, leading to these general experiential shifts:

          • Cognitions: more balanced, open, curious, spontaneous
          • Emotions: more connected, caring, empathetic, compassionate
          • Sensations: more warmth, spaciousness, ease
          • Impulses: more connection to self, others, and environment; co-regulation

          You won't and can't permanently live in safety. That's not the goal. Your system is supposed to flow amongst all of your Polyvagal states. But you can use the markers above to notice when you're in safety and then bring your mindful awareness to the felt experience of it.

          Safety typically shows up as one of the mixed state, regulated forms below. It's either more mobile or immobile.

          Sympathetic + safety = play

          Sympathetic isn't only fight-or-flight. With enough safety in the system, the same activation shows up as play.

          Cognitions
          Quick, curious, generative, spontaneous, imaginative, creating, humorous. Ideas flow easily and without judgment.
          Emotions
          Excited, joyful, fun, energized, engaged. The warm version of activation.
          Sensations
          Faster heart, mobilized energy, alert, flow, bouncy, rhythmic. But with warmth and openness, not tightness or pressure.
          Impulses
          To produce, create, move, smile, laugh, engage with others. The energy wants to go out into something fun and with safe others.

          Play looks like laughing hard with a friend, losing yourself in a creative project, dancing, the energy of exercise that feels good rather than punishing. Flow states. Productive intensity. Even healthy conflict, the kind where two people work through something charged and come out closer.

          Adults are starved for play, though they may not frame it that way. But mobilized connection with others? Yes.

          Play involves another. But if we remove the other, one can still exist in a state of sympathetic + safety. But if alone, I'd call this motivation.

          The same autonomic state that powers anxiety also powers joy. It just needs a sprinkling of safety in the mix.

          Dorsal + safety = stillness

          Stillness is dorsal in its regulated form. Dorsal is the same autonomic branch that produces shutdown, just with enough safety in the system to show up warm instead of cold. Connected instead of disconnected. Full instead of empty.

          Cognitions
          Connected to the present, aware of sensory input and internal experiences, contemplative, spacious, quiet. The mental chatter eases.
          Emotions
          Calm, relaxed, present, curious, content, appreciative.
          Sensations
          Warmth, internal ease and quiet, settled, soft.
          Impulses
          To rest, to be held, to drop deeper, to be immobile, use senses mindfully, connect with inner world.

          Stillness looks like curling up with a book, blanket, and tea. The drift of falling asleep in a safe place. The quiet, spacious state you sometimes find in meditation. Sitting by water, watching a fire, lying in grass.

          You're allowed to be in stillness. Stillness does not equal non-productivity. Instead, it's the necessary mindful collapse before and after work. Give yourself permission to rest in this regulated form of dorsal and to recognize the difference between stillness (warm, settled, present) and shutdown (cold, distant, absent).

          Stillness is alone. But stillness with a co-regulative other is called intimacy.

          The long arc

          Tracking your nervous system patterns

          Daily check-ins build a short-term feedback loop. Over weeks and months, a longer arc emerges; patterns you can't see in any single check-in.

          A few things worth tracking, even informally:

          Time-of-day patterns. Your state pattern may map to the clock. Mornings might tilt dorsal. Afternoons might tilt sympathetic. Evenings might shift again. Knowing your daily curve means you can stop interpreting normal fluctuation as proof something is wrong. And perhaps instead embrace your body's potential for these predictable times.

          Situational triggers. Certain situations reliably move you toward certain states. Particular meetings. Particular phone calls. Particular times of the year. Particular people. Tracking which situations push you which direction gives you the potential to intentionally prepare your system proactively.

          Relational patterns. Some people regulate you. Some people dysregulate you. Once you can see it, you can make different choices about exposure and recovery. You can set up proactive preparation and intentional recovery.

          Recovery time. When you do drop into a stuck state, how long does it take to come back? Months ago it might have been days. With practice, it may become hours. Tracking this gives you evidence that the practice is working.

          The early signals you used to miss. Most stuck states have a "ramp-up" phase that's easy to miss when you're not paying attention. Mild irritation that's about to become full sympathetic activation. Mild fog that's about to become full dorsal drop. Learning your own early signals means you can intervene with safety inputs while there's still ramp left to interrupt.

          None of this requires a tracking app or a journal. It just requires the daily check-ins, plus a willingness to notice patterns when they appear. The patterns will appear on their own.

          When it's blocked

          When you can't read your nervous system

          There will be times when you check in and find nothing. You're numb. You're foggy. You're so activated that the columns are all maxed out and you can't pick one signal out from the noise. The doors are all closed.

          This is useful information, too.

          When you can't read yourself, you're likely in an overwhelmed state of freeze. At this point, everything is too much, so using the columns may not be accessible.

          What to do in those moments:

          Don't force the read. Trying harder to understand or feel things you can't currently access can deepen the overwhelm and frustration. The attempt becomes another demand on a system that's already overloaded.

          Reach for co-regulation. A safe person or a pet. Borrowing someone else's nervous system is faster than trying to self-regulate when your own dashboard is offline. It might be enough to share a hug or just be in the same space with that safe other.

          Use movement. When the system is too dysregulated in freeze or flight/fight, intentional and mindful movement might be best. There is no prescriptive movement. Just move in a way that feels good enough. Maybe it's a walk. Maybe it's squeezing and releasing your fists. But be as mindful as possible. Actually pay attention to and feel the experience of movement.

          Wait for the columns to come back. They will. Stuck states release with time and safety. When the columns reopen, the read becomes possible again. You may benefit more from reflective nervous system reading after you have returned to your baseline.

          The companion pillar, The three stuck states, goes deep on what each stuck state looks like and what coming out of each one actually involves.

          For helpers

          For clinicians and helpers

          If you're a therapist, coach, somatic practitioner, or other helper, this page is built to be teachable.

          A few things to note:

          It's structured as a daily practice, not a single-session intervention. Nervous system literacy compounds. Clients who do brief daily check-ins for a month build observational fluency that's hard to develop in 50-minute sessions alone. Small, sustainable homework.

          The four-column structure is ideal for baseline reflection. Sure, a client can try and use it during mild dysregulation. Maybe even moderate. But the most benefit comes from intentional reflection when at a baseline.

          It pairs with the Current model. For clients new to polyvagal concepts, route them through The Polyvagal Current first. For clients in active stuckness, The three stuck states is a more useful entry. But they need the basic Polyvagal Theory knowledge first.

          The page is freely linkable. Use it however serves your clients. Attribution appreciated.

          Quick answers

          FAQ

          How long does it take to learn to read your own nervous system?

          The first reads start working within days. Real fluency builds over months and years. Like any literacy, the first words are slow and the reading deepens over time.

          What if I can never feel my body?

          Body access can be built, but it isn't required for nervous system literacy. Many people who've been dissociated from their bodies for years read themselves through cognitions and emotions. Use whichever column is open; the others come online as the practice builds.

          Is this the same as mindfulness?

          Related, but different. Mindfulness teaches present-moment awareness in general. This practice is more specific: it teaches you to read four columns (cognitions, emotions, sensations, impulses) and map what you find to the states of the Polyvagal Current. The two practices reinforce each other.

          What if my check-ins are inaccurate?

          They will be at first. That's fine. Reading your own nervous system is a probability skill, not a precision one. Over time, the reads get more accurate. Wrong reads are still information and still practice.

          Can I do this without a therapist?

          Yes. Nervous system literacy is a self-knowledge practice. A therapist can deepen it, especially if you have trauma history or significant dissociation, but the basic practice is something you can do on your own.

          Do I need to do this forever?

          No. The literacy becomes automatic over time. What starts as a deliberate check-in becomes background awareness. You'll still benefit from occasional deliberate check-ins, but the practice eventually integrates.
